. It is the simple memorization loop with a self-attention layer in front of the dense output. One random input of shape

children.html: 3×83 \times 83×8

children.value: is drawn once and trained toward the same two-component target as

program mha_simple
  use nf, only: dense, input, network, sgd, self_attention, flatten
  implicit none
  type(network) :: net
  real, allocatable :: x(:, :), y(:)
  integer, parameter :: num_iterations = 500
  integer :: n

  print '("Simple")'
  print '(60("="))'

  net = network([ &
    input(3, 8), &
    self_attention(4), &
    flatten(), &
    dense(2) &
  ])

  call net % print_info()

  allocate(x(3, 8))
  call random_number(x)

  y = [0.123456, 0.246802]
is a sequence of length 3 and a model width of 8.
asks for four heads. The head width has to divide the model width. The library sets

children.html: dk=84=2d_k = \frac{8}{4} = 2dk​=48​=2

children.value: and stops if the division is not exact. Each head computes scaled dot-product attention. With

children.html: QQQ
KKK
VVV

children.value: the slices of the query, key, and value for that head,

children.html: Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax ⁣(QKTdk)V.\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V.Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QKT​)V.

children.value: The scale in the source is

children.html: 1/dk\sqrt{1/d_k}1/dk​​

children.value: , which is the same factor. The attention matrix for a head is

children.html: 3×33 \times 33×3

children.value: on this run reports 288 attention parameters. That count is three input projections and one output projection, each an

children.html: 8×88 \times 88×8

children.value: matrix plus a bias of length 8:

children.html: 3(8⋅8+8)+(8⋅8+8)=288.3(8 \cdot 8 + 8) + (8 \cdot 8 + 8) = 288.3(8⋅8+8)+(8⋅8+8)=288.
3×83 \times 83×8

children.value: attention output into a vector of length 24.

children.html: 24⋅2+2=5024 \cdot 2 + 2 = 5024⋅2+2=50

children.value: parameters and a sigmoid activation. The attention layer’s activation field is blank in the print. The nonlinearity inside it is the softmax over the attention scores.

do n = 0, num_iterations

    call net % forward(x)
    call net % backward(y)
    call net % update(optimizer=sgd(learning_rate=1.))

    if (mod(n, 50) == 0) &
      print '(i4,2(3x,f8.6))', n, net % predict(x)

once, before the loop, so every step sees the same input. The target is again

children.html: (0.123456, 0.246802)(0.123456,\ 0.246802)(0.123456, 0.246802)

children.value: with the default quadratic loss, and SGD with learning rate 1. The print is

program mha_simple
  use nf, only: dense, input, network, sgd, self_attention, flatten
  implicit none
  type(network) :: net
  real, allocatable :: x(:, :), y(:)
  integer, parameter :: num_iterations = 500
  integer :: n

  print '("Simple")'
  print '(60("="))'

  net = network([ &
    input(3, 8), &
    self_attention(4), &
    flatten(), &
    dense(2) &
  ])

  call net % print_info()

  allocate(x(3, 8))
  call random_number(x)

  y = [0.123456, 0.246802]

  do n = 0, num_iterations

    call net % forward(x)
    call net % backward(y)
    call net % update(optimizer=sgd(learning_rate=1.))

    if (mod(n, 50) == 0) &
      print '(i4,2(3x,f8.6))', n, net % predict(x)

  end do

end program mha_simple

Step 0 prints 0.476483 and 0.484180, near the middle of the sigmoid range. At step 500 the outputs are 0.123610 and 0.246802. The second component matches the target at six decimals. The first is still

children.html: 1.5×10−41.5 \times 10^{-4}1.5×10−4

children.value: high. The dense network on the simple page matched both components by step 450. Attention has more parameters, and it is not a faster way to memorize one constant.
is enough to put a transformer block’s attention into the same
loop as a dense network. The input shape fixes the sequence length and the model width, and the head count has to divide the width.
